sections.title: Preface
fragments: Understand the operations. Then make better engineering decisions.
Why this book starts with foundations

Building an AI feature can look simple: send text to a model and display the result. The difficult questions appear soon afterward. What information did the model receive? Why did an input use so many tokens? What can a similarity score tell us? Which part of a memory estimate belongs to the model, and which part belongs to the application?

This book builds the tools for answering those questions. It starts with numbers and representations, follows how learning changes parameters, and then traces how a Transformer combines context. Each chapter asks you to calculate something small enough to check, rather than memorize a component name.
A foundation for a wider engineering practice

AI engineering also involves data choices, evaluation, retrieval, application design, permissions, deployment and operational care. Understanding a model does not replace those responsibilities. It helps you separate what the model calculates from what the surrounding system must guarantee.
These chapters develop mathematical and model foundations. Wider systems topics are connections and next steps, not additional lessons already taught here.
Learn through a sequence you can reproduce

A definition is useful only when you can use it. We move from an intuitive question to a visible example, then name the operation and calculate its result. Symbols are explained where they enter the lesson. Exercises and interview questions include reasoning, not just an answer key.

Small examples deliberately leave out much of a trained model. Their purpose is to expose the mechanics and the assumptions. A successful calculation is evidence that you followed the operation; it is not evidence that a real system is accurate, safe or ready for production.

Use the book as a working notebook. Predict an output, write down the intermediate values, and compare your result with the explanation. A mistake in a tiny example is inexpensive and often reveals exactly which idea needs another pass.

sections.title: How to use this book
fragments: Read with a pencil or a small program

You need basic arithmetic, not a prior course in linear algebra or calculus. Familiarity with arrays, loops and functions helps with the code. We explain mathematical notation separately from programming notation.
You can read without running code. When you do run an example, predict its output first, then compare the result with your reasoning.

Read the first two chapters before the model calculations: they teach vectors, matrices, rates of change and gradients. Tokenization explains how text becomes IDs. Embeddings explain how IDs become usable representations. Neural networks build the forward and backward calculations. The Transformer chapter joins the parts, and the attention chapter examines matching, masks, caching and execution more closely.
If you already know a topic, use the
to find it. Do not skip a worked example merely because its vocabulary is familiar. Being able to calculate the example is a stronger check than recognizing its name.
What question does this operation answer?
Name the coordinates, shapes, units and assumptions.
Write the intermediate values before looking at the result.
Say what the result tells you and what it does not tell you.
Try exercises with the answer hidden, then compare the reasoning. All exercise and interview answers are included in the EPUB and complete PDFs. Website answers can be expanded individually.

The website has interactive experiments. The offline HTML uses local assets and native expandable answers. The EPUB is reflowable: text adjusts to the reader's page and type settings. Its diagrams and formula images can be enlarged; some ebook readers handle wide images and tables differently. The complete reading PDF has fixed pages and selectable prose. The print interior has a smaller fixed page with a binding margin.

In static editions, interactive controls are removed and the written examples remain. Keep a calculator handy for logarithms, exponentials and trigonometry. Reported decimals are rounded; use the exact expressions when comparing two calculation paths.

The Language of LLMs: Vectors, Matrices, and Meaning
A language for representing information, transforming it, and deciding what to combine.
Start here: no linear algebra assumed
Worked examples + an interactive lab
The question we are answering
A language model receives token IDs and produces scores for the next token. What mathematical objects carry the information between those two points?

Imagine building a search feature for a support center. Someone types, "I can't access my account." A useful result might say "Reset your sign-in credentials," even though the words differ. Exact string matching is not enough. We need a numerical representation that makes useful comparisons possible.
Linear algebra gives us ways to store and work with those numbers:
. Training adjusts the numbers so these operations become useful for a task. Arithmetic alone does not give a model an understanding of language.
By the end, you will be able to trace tensor shapes through one attention head, distinguish similarity from dependence, and explain why a small low-rank update can adapt a large weight matrix.

Principal component analysis
(PCA) chooses unit, mutually perpendicular directions of greatest variance. Perpendicular is also called

. Eigenvalues of a covariance matrix give the variance retained along each such direction, and their sum gives total variance. Centering first prevents an arbitrary coordinate origin from dominating this spread calculation.

necessarily 90% of task-relevant information.
Singular value decomposition
(SVD) factors even a rectangular real matrix into input directions, stretches, and output directions:
Read the product from right to left, as with other column-vector transformations. First
measures the input along chosen perpendicular unit directions. Next
scales those coordinates by nonnegative numbers called
. It is a rectangular matrix with nonzero entries only on its main diagonal. Finally U combines the scaled coordinates along output directions.

The columns of U and V are orthonormal: each has length 1, and different columns are perpendicular. These are the full-factor shapes; software often uses smaller equivalent layouts. Unlike an eigenvector direction, an input singular-vector direction need not match its output direction. The input and output may even have different numbers of coordinates.
Worked example / Keep the stronger stretch
; subscripts on I give its row and column size. Input [2,4] first stays [2,4], then becomes [6,4,0], then stays there. The singular values are 3 and 1.
Keeping only stretch 3 gives

has one entry of 1 and all others zero. Its

That reconstruction guarantee is about matrix error, not downstream model quality. PCA can be computed through SVD of centered data; compression uses a few large stretches as a starting point, then measures task performance. A full treatment of numerical SVD algorithms is beyond this introductory bridge.
A covariance matrix has eigenvalues 8 and 2. How much variance does its first principal component retain? Does that guarantee the same fraction of useful label information?
. No. Variance measures spread, not usefulness for a particular prediction. A small-variance direction might contain the decisive signal.

These tools help analyze embedding collections, compression, and optimization curvature. A normal Transformer forward pass does not need to compute determinants, inverses, or eigendecompositions at each token. Learn them to reason about structure, not because they are all steps in inference.
Try each question before opening the solution. A useful answer includes both the number and an explanation of what it represents.
01 / Representation is not rank
A table contains 1,000 embeddings of width 64. What is its shape and maximum possible rank? Must its rank equal 64?
; maximum rank is 64. Its actual rank may be smaller if columns or rows are dependent. Coordinate width and measured rank are not the same.
Use 4 tokens, input width 6, query/key width 2, and value width 3. Give the shapes of
. How many positions can the first causal query attend to?
. The first query can attend to only its own position, assuming the usual inclusive causal mask.
03 / Similarity versus dependence
dependent? What is their cosine similarity, approximately?
They are independent: no scalar multiple of the first creates a nonzero second coordinate. Cosine similarity is
. Near alignment does not create exact dependence.
04 / Can a projection be reversed?
matrix maps a 5-coordinate row vector to 2 coordinates. Can every input be uniquely reconstructed from the result?

No. The rank is at most 2, so the mapping cannot preserve all five independent input directions. Different inputs must share outputs. Extra assumptions about a restricted input set could permit reconstruction there, but not for all of
weight update, compare dense parameters with rank-4 factor parameters. Then explain why this does not prove a specific training-memory saving.
. The dense count is about 10.67 times larger. Actual memory also includes frozen weights, activations, gradients, optimizer states, precision choices, and other trainable components.
9. Your mental model, upgraded
Represent. Transform. Combine.
A vector's width counts coordinates; a collection's rank counts independent directions.
A dot product combines length and alignment. Cosine removes length for nonzero vectors.
A matrix mixes coordinates; its shape tells you which inputs and outputs are possible.
Attention computes query-key scores and uses normalized weights to combine values.
Low rank constrains an update. Eigenvectors and singular vectors reveal useful structure.
You can now read the forward arithmetic of a small network. The next question is more interesting:
how should its weights change when the prediction is wrong?
That is where calculus enters.

The small exact matrices teach the operations and their conditions. SVD remains a worked introductory bridge, not a numerical-algorithm course; matrix reconstruction guarantees do not establish downstream model quality.

How LLMs Learn: Derivatives, Gradients, and Optimization
A language for measuring sensitivity, tracing responsibility, and turning error into a better next step.
Prerequisite: chapter 01; no calculus assumed
Worked examples + two interactive labs
The question we are answering
A model made the wrong prediction. Which weights should change, in which direction, and by how much?

In chapter 1, matrices were transformations we already had. Training reverses that perspective: the weights become adjustable inputs to a loss function. Calculus tells us how sensitive that loss is to each weight.
Imagine tuning a delivery-time estimator. If every estimate is too low, increasing one coefficient might help. But with many interacting coefficients, guessing is slow. A
tells us how a small change affects the result at the current setting. A
gathers that information for many parameters.
calculates the gradients efficiently, and an
uses them to change the parameters. We will build these ideas one at a time.

Our examples begin with tiny functions that can be checked by hand. We often choose smooth curves: no corners, jumps, or abruptly changing slopes in the region being studied. Real LLM losses depend on many parameters and data, with much more complicated landscapes than one bowl. The small examples isolate the mechanism, not the full difficulty of training.
1. Functions, composition, and limits
A function is a rule that gives one output for each permitted input. For example,
maps 3 to 9 and -3 to 9. Inputs need not have distinct outputs. The

does, but still return one output. Mathematical functions describe dependencies; unlike arbitrary code, they do not have hidden mutable state.
Three function families recur in model mathematics: affine rules such as
model squared error; and exponentials and logarithms connect scores to probabilities and loss. A graph puts inputs on the horizontal axis and outputs on the vertical axis.

The affine rule increases by 2 whenever x increases by 1. Squaring bends: the change from 0 to 1 is 1, but from 1 to 2 it is 3. The

Negative powers of e give numbers between 0 and 1, so those numbers have negative logarithms. For example,

If a curve approaches 4 from both sides at x = 2 but is assigned value 100 there, does its limit become 100?

No. The limit stays 4. The value 100 breaks continuity at the point, and differentiability there is impossible. Training frameworks use derivative rules for their operations; they do not run a numerical limit loop on every update.
2. A derivative is local sensitivity

If a service charges a flat $2 per request, one more request adds $2. Its rate of change is constant. But on a curved cost or loss function, the rate depends on where you are. A derivative measures that instantaneous rate, rather than an average over a large interval.

6. From logits to a training signal
At one position, a vocabulary projection gives one raw score per candidate token. These scores are

05 / Stationary is not optimal

06 / Explain a training step without jargon
Describe the distinct jobs of a forward pass, loss, backpropagation, and optimizer. Which of them normally changes weights?

The forward pass computes predictions using current weights. Loss scores those predictions against targets. Backpropagation computes local loss sensitivities for parameters. The optimizer uses them and its update rule to change weights. Ordinary generation normally keeps the weights fixed.
10. From arithmetic to learning
Predict. Measure. Differentiate. Update.
A derivative measures local sensitivity, not output value or guaranteed finite change.
A gradient gathers partial derivatives; its dot product with a displacement predicts local loss change.
Backpropagation multiplies sensitivities along paths and adds contributions from branches.
An optimizer updates weights. Its step size matters as much as the direction.
Softmax plus cross-entropy produces the logit signal "prediction minus target."
Curvature, noise, and the data distribution limit what one local gradient can tell you.

Linear algebra gives a language for the forward computation. Calculus gives a language for how that computation responds to change. Together, they let you reason about an LLM as an engineered numerical system, rather than a collection of mysterious formulas.

Accumulation, antiderivatives, densities, and expectations provide worked background, not a complete integration course. Numerical examples explain local sensitivity and update rules; they do not guarantee convergence or establish the best optimizer for a production model.

From Text to Tokens: How LLMs Read Language
Follow a message from characters to vocabulary entries, then calculate what those choices cost in context, memory, and engineering complexity.
Prerequisite: basic arithmetic; chapters 01-02 provide connections
Original diagrams + fully worked algorithms
The question we are answering
Your application sends a short message, yet the API reports many tokens. What exactly did the model receive, and why does the answer depend on the tokenizer?
Your application starts with text, but a language model needs numbers. A

connects the two. It splits text into pieces and gives each piece a numerical ID from a fixed vocabulary. It follows rules about the text and the available pieces; it does not need to understand the sentence first.

The word "read" in this chapter's title means this input conversion, not human comprehension. We will build small tokenizers you can trace with a pencil, distinguish their assumptions from real implementations, and connect their output to the matrices and learning machinery of the earlier chapters. No probability or Unicode knowledge is assumed.
How to work through this chapter

First learn the units and lookup contract in sections 1-2, then trace the three algorithms in sections 3-7. Sections 8-11 connect them to model storage and application requests. In section 6, understand the three-path example before continuing into the more demanding dynamic-programming, logarithm, and estimation calculations; they explain implementation choices, not prerequisites for recognizing a token. Each section has an explained check so you can test your reasoning before moving on.
1. Text, characters, bytes, and tokens are different units
Imagine storing the customer message

is a linguistic unit; spaces and punctuation help a human recognize words in this English example. But spaces are not universal word boundaries. Chinese text, source code, email addresses, and product identifiers all challenge a simple "split on spaces" rule.
" can mean different things. What looks like one character on screen may contain several text elements. This visible unit is called a
gives text elements numbered addresses called
is capital A. The part after U+ uses base sixteen: after digits 0 through 9, it uses A through F. A code point identifies a text element; it is not a byte.
contains eight bits. Each bit has two choices, so a byte has
possible patterns, numbered 0 through 255. The exponent 8 means multiply eight factors of 2.

turns code points into bytes for storage or transmission. UTF-8 uses one to four bytes for each permitted Unicode code point. There is one boundary worth knowing: Unicode reserves numbers called surrogates for UTF-16's internal encoding rules. A surrogate on its own is not a valid UTF-8 text character.
One visible letter can have different underlying representations
e followed by a combining acute accent
The last two rows can look the same while containing different code points and bytes.

is a declared text transformation that puts equivalent forms into a chosen representation. For example, Unicode NFC normalization combines this e-plus-accent into the precomposed form. A tokenizer may normalize, lowercase, or preserve text; its configuration decides. Lowercasing
is a separate, potentially information-losing transformation, not a necessary consequence of Unicode normalization.
Worked example / Count the unit you mean
using precomposed é, there are two code points and
. A raw byte tokenizer would emit three ordinary tokens. A toy vocabulary containing the entire byte sequence for
could instead emit one token. Neither count is a count of English words. In JavaScript,
counts UTF-16 code units, another storage unit; do not assume it counts graphemes, Unicode code points, UTF-8 bytes, or model tokens.

is one unit recognized by a particular tokenizer. Ordinary text tokens can cover a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, whitespace, or several of these together. Byte tokens can even cover less than a complete Unicode character. Special tokens, introduced in
, represent structure rather than ordinary text.
Predict / Same appearance, same count?
Without normalization, must the two accent spellings above produce the same tokens? What changes if both are normalized to NFC first?

No. Their byte inputs differ, so a byte-based tokenizer can produce different IDs and counts. NFC makes these particular inputs identical before segmentation, so a deterministic tokenizer with the same configuration then produces the same result. Decoding cannot tell which original spelling was used after that distinction has been removed.
2. A vocabulary is a contract, not a dictionary of meanings
is the finite collection of token entries available to the tokenizer. A
is an integer identifying one entry. A
spells something different from
means choosing the ordered pieces that cover an input. In our displays,
means two tokens, not text containing a vertical bar or an inserted space. Similarly,
shows three character tokens from
; the separating spaces are diagram notation. Literal spaces in input will be called out explicitly. A saved tokenizer
contains its vocabulary and the rules and settings needed to repeat its behavior.
A deliberately tiny vocabulary; IDs are local to this example
looks up the entries and reconstructs

. ID 7 is not seven units of meaning. Its distance from ID 3 does not measure similarity. Renumbering this vocabulary is safe only if all dependent model rows, output classes, and special-token settings are updated consistently.
The ID tells the model which stored numbers to retrieve. Those numbers form an
: an ordered list, also called a vector. Each value in that list is a
stores these lists in a rectangular table, one row per ID and one column per coordinate. Each stored number is a model
, or weight, that training can adjust. The model's Transformer layers then process the retrieved vectors. You do not need to know their internal design to follow a row lookup.
Segmentation, ID lookup, and embedding lookup have distinct jobs. Every ID and vector here is invented.
Why not store every word? A word-only dictionary must handle new names, typos, code, and word variations; an unseen word may become an
item, abbreviated OOV. A character-level system reuses smaller pieces but usually needs longer sequences, and a finite character inventory can still miss a character. A
system reuses pieces smaller than words while retaining larger common units. A piece is not guaranteed to be a grammatical root or suffix.
Three hypothetical encodings of maps
An unseen word may map to UNK and lose its spelling
Long sequences; missing characters without fallback
Segmentation depends on vocabulary and procedure
A compiler lexer is a useful analogy: both turn text into units. But a programming-language lexer recognizes a specified grammar, whereas many LLM tokenizers learn reusable units from a
, a collection of training text. Neither operation alone is semantic understanding.
Do not confuse three different activities
builds the vocabulary and splitting rules from a corpus. Once saved, these rules can be reused.
use that saved tokenizer; a new user message normally does not change it.

is a separate job. It adjusts the model's stored numbers, including embedding values, to improve predictions. During ordinary generation, neither the tokenizer nor the model weights change. The model chooses new output tokens using what has already been trained.

Tokenizer decoding turns IDs back into text; it does not choose a reply. During

Serving documentation sometimes calls this repeated generation phase "decode" too. Check whether the term means choosing new IDs or turning existing IDs into text.
Predict / New spelling or new training?
entry. Must an application train a new tokenizer to encode it?
No, provided its encoding rules can produce

3. BPE training: count, merge, recount
Imagine a log compressor that repeatedly notices the same adjacent fragments. Replacing two fragments with one saves one sequence position at each non-overlapping occurrence.
, or BPE, began as a compression method; tokenizer training adapts the pair-merging idea to build reusable units. Despite the historical name, our first example starts with characters, not bytes.
means immediately next to each other in the current sequence. A pair's
is its occurrence count, including repeated corpus entries. A
replaces a selected adjacent pair with one combined token. The new entry is added to the vocabulary; old entries remain usable. A
records its order in training, with a smaller rank meaning an earlier merge.
Exact assumptions for this teaching tokenizer
once. We process entries in that order. We start with the six characters

; there are no boundary tokens or special tokens. Pairs never cross entry boundaries. On equal frequency, select the pair first encountered while scanning these entries from left to right. Replace non-overlapping occurrences from left to right. Stop after five merges. These deterministic rules make this example reproducible; they are not a specification for every BPE library.

We can store each unique entry once with its frequency. This is equivalent to repeating it in the corpus. To count a pair, count occurrences within each entry, multiply by that entry's frequency, and add. For example,
appears once in each entry, so its total is

they denote an ordered pair of tokens.
Initial pair counts: every adjacent pair is accounted for
Corpus sequences become shorter while the dictionary becomes larger. The frequency weights do not change.

Audit the sequence savings and vocabulary growth
Weighted token occurrences
{m, a, p, s, l, e, ma, map, maps, mapl, maple}
has no special linguistic meaning. It exists because of the counts and tie-breaking rule, not because the algorithm discovered a meaningful word part, called a morpheme.
Overlaps make "count" different from "replace"

tokens. That is one actual replacement and one position saved. Libraries can differ in training details; do not assume pair count always equals immediate token savings when pairs overlap.
Production tokenizer training uses vastly larger corpora, targets, and implementation machinery. The enduring mechanism is to count the
units, add a merged entry, and update the representation. A vocabulary target must leave room for base and special entries; training may stop early if no useful pair remains.

Immediately after rank 2, should

No. The current sequences contain

counts 5 and still wins rank 3. Counts describe the corpus supplied, not a timeless property of a word.
4. BPE encoding, byte coverage, and decoding

Training saves a vocabulary and an ordered merge list. Encoding uses that list; it does not learn new merges from the user's message. For our toy encoder, start with separate characters. Find neighboring pairs that have a saved merge rule. Apply the rule with the smallest rank, then check the new sequence again. Stop when no saved rule applies. If the chosen pair occurs more than once, replace non-overlapping occurrences from left to right, as in training.
Worked example / Encode using a frozen prefix of the training
Freeze training after rank 2. The available merges are

Merge-rank BPE is not generally interchangeable with "take the longest string in the vocabulary." Greedy longest-match is a different encoding rule, used in the WordPiece example below. Record the algorithm as well as the vocabulary. Preprocessing, boundaries, and rank order are all part of a reproducible BPE encoding.
Worked example / Two eligible merges compete
Use a separate toy vocabulary

What if a base unit is missing?
The six-character toy cannot losslessly encode

: d is missing. It must reject that input or follow an explicit unknown-unit policy. It would be wrong to silently invent d, a new ID, or a new merge. The same issue affects an alphabet trained without a newly encountered script.

begins with all 256 byte values, then learns merges over byte sequences. With that complete base vocabulary, any byte sequence can be decomposed into available units, even if no larger learned token matches. UTF-8 gives ordinary valid Unicode text a byte representation. This solves base-byte coverage, not semantic comprehension or equal efficiency across languages.

is a related but distinct configuration: a tokenizer whose normal units are characters or subwords can fall back to byte entries for an uncovered portion. It must actually include and enable those entries. Not every Unigram or SentencePiece tokenizer does. An
token instead says "unknown"; once spelling is replaced with it, exact reconstruction is usually impossible.
Worked example / Reconstruct bytes before decoding text
Suppose a byte vocabulary emits separate byte tokens for precomposed é with payloads
is the byte content stored in an entry; these byte values are not necessarily its token ID. Concatenating the payloads gives

, a valid UTF-8 encoding of é. Neither byte alone is a complete UTF-8 character. Decoding them independently as text can produce an error or replacement character. During inspection, show raw bytes; during streaming, keep incomplete UTF-8 fragments buffered until the sequence is complete. A model can also generate a byte sequence that is not valid UTF-8, so the decoder's error policy matters.

is a deliberate ordinary-content experiment setting, not a recommendation to accept privileged special IDs from users.
Optional comparison: WordPiece and a SentencePiece-based artifact

Missing environment values intentionally stop this optional example until you supply revisions. Compare the displayed continuation and whitespace markers. For real chat accounting use the model's supported chat-template or API counting path, including tool definitions and any non-text parts. The downloadable packages and model files are not bundled with this offline book, and these optional experiments are not claimed as measurements made for this edition.

In .NET, the same engineering contract applies: use a supported tokenizer implementation for the exact model and artifact, pin versions, measure the fully assembled request, and compare with serving usage. A package-specific .NET implementation is outside this chapter.
Predict / What would make a fair comparison?
A WordPiece output has two extra special tokens and lowercases text; another tokenizer preserves case and adds none. What must you record before comparing counts?

Record exact input, artifact revisions, normalization, whether special tokens were added, and whether you measured plain text or a complete request. Separate ordinary-text efficiency from required structural overhead. Do not interpret equal counts as equal IDs, semantic quality, or model compatibility.
12. Work it through and explain it aloud
Use these questions for practice or interview preparation. Explain what happens, why it happens, and where the explanation stops applying. An algorithm name alone is not enough.
With the weighted corpus from section 3, stop after rank 1. List all pair counts and predict rank 2. What is the vocabulary size after that second merge?

04 / Best path is not total likelihood

06 / Padding and structural cost
Three sequences have lengths 2, 4, and 5. Right-pad to the longest. How many positions are padding, and what fraction of the rectangle is that? Is PAD necessarily the same ID as EOS?

07 / Design a budget failure policy

A 16,000-token service has 13,500 input tokens and a requested output allowance of 3,000. Explain what you would change, what you would recount, and why "persistent memory" does not solve the immediate overflow.

Planned use is 16,500, so remove at least 500 tokens or reduce output by at least 500 if the task and provider permit; practical headroom may call for more. Prefer reducing low-priority retrieval/history at safe boundaries. Re-serialize and recount instructions, template, schemas, selected content, and output allowance. External memory stores omitted information but does not make it available in the current inference unless it is retrieved into the bounded context.
08 / Explain the complete path without jargon
Explain how text reaches a model, compare the three algorithms, and follow a tool call back to an answer. Include why whitespace, language, and model compatibility matter.

A configured tokenizer transforms text, segments it with an existing vocabulary, and maps pieces to IDs. BPE learns merges; WordPiece uses a useful subword vocabulary with commonly greedy encoding; Unigram estimates and prunes pieces while considering alternative paths. A framework such as SentencePiece can supply more than one algorithm. IDs select learned embedding rows rather than measuring meaning. Whitespace, scripts, and code patterns alter available pieces and counts. A compatible chat format includes role and boundary information. A generated tool request must be validated and executed by the runtime, with a result supplied to a later model pass. Budget the actual compatible tokenized request, not words or another model's counts.
13. The boundary between strings and numerical models
Represent. Segment. Identify. Look up.
Visible characters, code points, bytes, words, and tokens count different things.
Training constructs a tokenizer; encoding uses it; model training learns numerical parameters.
BPE merge ranks, WordPiece greedy matching, and Unigram path scoring are different procedures.
Complete byte coverage prevents missing base bytes, not missing knowledge or uneven efficiency.
Vocabulary size affects embedding storage and output classes as well as sequence lengths.
Special tokens and templates express structure; the runtime owns tool execution and authorization.
Measure the actual model-compatible request, including overhead, output allowance, and repeated retrieval text.
You can now trace a tokenizer's choices rather than treating token counts as mysterious API trivia.

From Tokens to Meaning: How Embeddings Represent Language
Trace a token into a learned vector, calculate similarity, and discover how position changes the representations a model can use.
Prerequisite: arithmetic; concise reminders of chapters 01-03
Original diagrams + explained calculations
The question we are answering

Your search box receives "extend program enrollment," but the useful document says "renew membership." How can numerical representations help connect those phrases? And why does reversing "service calls client" change a sentence even when its tokens stay the same?
Chapter 3 turned text into token IDs. What can a model do with an ID? First, it uses the ID to retrieve a list of numbers called an
: a way to record information about an item. Training makes the numbers useful for the model's task. Subtracting or multiplying the IDs themselves does not reveal meaning.
Preparing for an interview? First work through the explanations, then use the
interview questions and reasoned answers
to practice explaining the model's boundaries aloud.

"Meaning" in this title means useful statistical representations of language, not proof of human understanding. We will distinguish token lookup, context-dependent representations, and whole-text vectors. Every vector and score in this chapter is an invented teaching example, not output measured from a production model.

Sections 1-6 build the representation and retrieval story. Sections 7-12 teach order, angles, sine and cosine, learned positions, RoPE, and masking from the ground up. Sections 13-16 consolidate implementation choices, practice, interview preparation, and the recap. A complete embedding-model training recipe is beyond this chapter.

4. Vector offsets are hypotheses, not semantic laws
In a map, subtracting one location from another gives a displacement. Likewise, subtracting embedding vectors can reveal a direction of change in a learned representation.

5. The same lookup can lead to different contextual states

Compare "the loan came from the bank" with "the stream passed the bank." Assume the tokenizer gives bank the same ID in both. Its initial table row is then identical. Check that assumption in real text: whitespace or a different split can change the ID.

We put loan and stream before bank for a reason. A causal decoder can use preceding text, but cannot use a later word to change an earlier state in that pass. A bidirectional encoder can use permitted words on both sides. Which context is available depends on the architecture.

These contribution weights, also called coefficients, are normally nonnegative and add to 1. They are calculated for the current input, not simply read from the stored model weights.
Each later layer works on the transformed results of the previous layer. A token's hidden state can therefore change with the surrounding text even though its starting table row is the same.

6. A whole-text embedding supports a retrieval pipeline

Mean pooling is one option, not a rule for every model. Other models use a designated summary position, a selected final state, or a learned output transformation. Follow the encoder's documented procedure; choosing a summary method yourself does not establish retrieval quality.

When a question arrives, encode it compatibly and compare it with the stored vectors. Rank candidates, enforce permissions, and select useful passage text.

06 / How can the same token acquire different representations in different sentences?
Separate the stored token row from the later contextual state, including the decoder's visibility limit.

The same vocabulary ID retrieves the same token-table row in a given saved model. Later layers calculate a hidden state: an intermediate vector that depends on that row and the context the architecture permits it to use. Thus bank can start with one stored row but acquire different states after finance-related versus river-related preceding text. A tokenizer can sometimes split a word differently; this explanation assumes the bank ID is the same.

A causal decoder can use earlier and current positions, not future text. Saying the bank state already knows a disambiguating word that only appears later would be incorrect for that architecture. Bidirectional encoders permit different visibility. Contextual states are newly computed values, not new sense-specific rows inserted into the vocabulary.
The chapter's toy mixtures show the arithmetic
; they illustrate context dependence, not the full Transformer layer.
07 / What does cosine similarity measure, and why use it for search?
Calculate a score and explain why it is neither a probability nor a truth test.

Cosine similarity compares the directions of two nonzero vectors. First multiply matching coordinates and add to obtain the dot product. Then divide by the product of their lengths; a length is the square root of the sum of squared coordinates. For our illustrative renew and extend rows:

Dividing out the lengths removes positive scaling, which is useful when the chosen encoder's relevant signal is directional. The score can rank compatible query and passage vectors. It is not "96% confidence," and aligned vectors do not establish agreement or factual correctness. A zero vector has length zero, making this division undefined. Choose the metric specified for the encoder and evaluate retrieval on the actual task; not every embedding system requires cosine.
08 / How do embeddings participate in retrieval-augmented generation?
Trace both the retrieval path and the text delivered to the answering model.
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

means retrieving supporting information and supplying it to a model that generates an answer. Split source documents into manageable chunks, encode each chunk with a configured whole-text encoder, and store its vector alongside its text and metadata. Encode the query compatibly, compare query and chunk vectors, filter for permissions and applicability, and select useful passages.
The answering LLM receives the selected passage

as context; the search vectors are not simply pasted in as its token-table rows. In our retrieval example, a high-scoring renewal passage is only a candidate: version, account applicability, and what the passage actually says still matter. Retrieval can miss evidence, and generation can misuse it. Token lookup learning alone does not establish a high-quality text-search encoder.
Follow the two paths and complete ranking example
09 / What does embedding width control?
Explain its storage tradeoff without confusing width, vocabulary size, or context length.

Width d is the number of coordinates in one vector. Vocabulary size V counts possible token rows; sequence length counts occurrences in an input. These are different quantities. More coordinates provide more representational capacity, but whether that improves a task depends on training and model design, not width alone.
A four-row table with width three stores
numbers. At four bytes per number, that is
bytes for values alone. Doubling width to six stores

bytes. Comparing two vectors also uses more coordinate products. Real storage includes other parameters and overhead. Do not change a deployed encoder's width arbitrarily and expect its existing index to remain compatible.
10 / Are embeddings parameters, activations, or both?
Distinguish stored embedding weights from computed representations.

A typical token embedding table is a trainable weight matrix: its stored coordinates are part of the model's parameters. "Weights" is not restricted to numbers that visibly multiply an input in a layer diagram. Lookup also uses learned parameters.
But not every value called an embedding is itself a stored parameter. A contextual hidden state or a returned sentence vector is a computed output, often called an

: a numerical value produced while processing an input. The parameters determine how it is calculated. A useful interview answer names the object rather than asserting that all embeddings are weights or that embeddings and weights are unrelated.
Learning changes parameters
a separate encoder produces text vectors
Position and attention / Questions 11-21
11 / Why does ordinary full self-attention need an order mechanism?
Explain why word order matters and how positions make it available. What changes under a causal mask?

Content-only, unmasked self-attention compares each token's query with every token's key and mixes their values. If you reorder all input rows, those relationships move with the corresponding tokens. The outputs are correspondingly reordered, not necessarily identical arrays. This property is called permutation equivariance: the computation follows a rearrangement rather than assigning original-position meaning to it.

Consequently, those content-only comparisons cannot encode that service precedes client in one sentence but follows it in another. Additive position vectors or relative position mechanisms supply order-dependent information. This is a claim about full content-only attention, not every possible Transformer. A causal mask allows only a prefix, so reordering changes which connections are permitted; it is already order-dependent, though not an absolute-position vector.
The symmetric-mixer calculation
12 / How do positional encoding and positional embeddings differ?
Explain the terminology before describing an implementation.

Positional encoding is the broader idea of making a model's computation depend on where tokens occur. Positional embeddings often means learned vectors retrieved by position index, but terminology varies: the name "Rotary Positional Embeddings" does not imply a learned position-table lookup. State the actual mechanism.
In an additive design, token row
plus illustrative position row

. Both rows must have matching width. Learned positions retrieve their row from a table; fixed sinusoidal positions instead generate a compatible row from the position index. This toy addition row is not claimed to come from the sinusoidal formula. Standard RoPE instead rotates query/key coordinate pairs inside attention. Those operations are not interchangeable additions to the same input row.
the architectural comparison
13 / How would you calculate a fixed sinusoidal position vector?
Give the coordinate pattern, a reproducible example, and its placement.

The convention taught here uses coordinate pairs with different angular rates. A rate tells you how many radians the angle advances per position; a radian measures an arc relative to the circle's radius. For even width d=4 and zero-based pair index i, the rate is
; the half power means square root. At zero-based position p=2, multiplying by those rates gives angles
Sine gives the vertical unit-circle coordinate and cosine the horizontal coordinate. Store sine then cosine for each pair, filling coordinates 0 through 3 in order:
The resulting position row is

. The trigonometric values are rounded; no row is learned in this fixed method. Add this row coordinate by coordinate to a width-four token row in the additive architecture. Multiple rates create patterns changing at different scales. Do not claim the short example proves unique positions for arbitrarily large indices or useful unlimited context.
14 / Why keep both sine and cosine in a position pair?
Give a concrete ambiguity that one coordinate alone would lose, then explain the shift relationship.
A unit circle has radius one. At angle 0 its horizontal/vertical coordinates are
; at a half turn, angle pi radians, they are
. Sine alone gives 0 at both angles. A stored
. Both coordinates together locate the point within one turn, though the pair repeats after a full turn.

A fixed angular shift transforms both coordinates by the same rotation rule at that rate. This gives systematic relationships between position pairs rather than independently assigned random rows. Multiple rates add different repeating scales; the learned network can use their patterns, but that is not a promise of perfect ordering at any length.
The circle drawing defines the functions
the shift derivation and p=1 to p=2 arithmetic
show why the two-coordinate relation works.
15 / How do learned positions differ from fixed sinusoidal positions?
Compare where values come from, training, storage, and untrained positions.

A learned position table has one row per supported position and one column per coordinate. Training adjusts its values through gradients from the model's loss, just as other parameters can be adjusted. The address is a position index, not a vocabulary ID. A fixed sinusoidal row comes from functions of the index and specified rates; the position functions themselves have no learned table parameters.
For four supported positions and width three, a learned table stores

values. Position 4 is outside its zero-based rows 0-3; there is no row to retrieve without a deliberate adaptation. A sinusoidal formula can calculate another index, but calculability does not mean the trained model uses that unfamiliar position well. Both methods still operate within the configured model.
The table, gradient paths, and extension example
make the distinction explicit.
16 / What operation does RoPE perform?
Describe a coordinate pair, angle, and resulting representation without invoking unexplained matrix notation.
Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)

turns two coordinates of a query or key as though turning a point in a plane. Position times the pair's angular rate determines how far it turns. Different pairs can use different rates. The rotation mixes each pair's existing content coordinates; it does not replace them with a standalone position row.
For a clearly nondefault illustration rate pi/4 radians per position, position 2 gives angle
. The formulas are new first coordinate
, where x,y are the old coordinates and theta is the turn angle. With x=1, y=0, cosine=0 and sine=1, they give
the four-coordinate example
uses the chapter's actual base convention.
17 / Where does standard RoPE enter attention?
Does it directly rotate stored token-table rows or values?

First a layer computes a query, key, and value from each hidden-state row through learned linear projections: multiply coordinates by learned coefficients and add. Queries express what a position is comparing, keys provide comparison candidates, and values supply the information mixed by attention.
The three explicit projection products

Standard RoPE rotates query and key pairs after those projections and before their dot-product comparison. It does not directly rotate the stored token table or the value vector in this convention. The changed scores still change the value mixture and later hidden states, so "RoPE has no effect on token representations" would also be misleading. Specify the layer and operation rather than trusting a loose diagram label.
Follow the original RoPE path diagram
18 / Why can RoPE express relative position?
Explain the shared-shift property and what remains dependent on token content.

Rotating a query at position m and a key at position n changes their dot product according to a rotation difference. With unchanged content pairs and the same pair rate, the positional factor depends on the signed gap

, not separately on both absolute indices. A shared shift of both indices preserves that gap. The complete score still depends on the original query/key content; equal gaps alone do not make arbitrary sentences produce identical attention scores.
and the separate toy rate pi/4, query 2/key 3 and query 5/key 6 both have gap 1. Their dot is
The transpose, cancellation, and composition derivation

proves the relative relationship beyond this example. RoPE avoids a learned row for each position and supplies a useful relative mechanism, but attention masks can block either comparison and long-context quality needs separate evidence.
19 / Why is a causal mask not a substitute for a position vector?
Separate what the two mechanisms contribute to an attention calculation.

Position handling changes representations or scores based on location. A causal mask restricts which keys a query is allowed to use during next-token prediction. For zero-based query position 1, keys 0 and 1 are allowed; key 2 is in its future and is excluded before normalizing attention weights. RoPE does not grant access to that future key.
the complete masked example
, permitted exponentiated scores are 1 and 2. Their sum is 3, so allowed weights are

; the blocked future weight is 0 regardless of its large score. The mask supplies order-dependent connectivity but not an explicit absolute index or sinusoidal coordinate. Both mechanisms can operate together; padding masks address yet another visibility condition.
20 / Does computable RoPE mean unlimited usable context?
Distinguish a mathematical position, supported input length, and tested model quality.

No. A rotation formula may accept another position index while a model or service imposes a finite context window: the number of tokens permitted in a request. Predictions can deteriorate beyond the training range even when the software accepts the input. More retained tokens also increase cache storage and attention work.

Scaling or interpolating positions changes the computation. For example, replacing p by p/2 changes angle p times rate into half that angle: position 2 at rate 1 changes from 2 radians to 1. That alone does not establish useful context extension. Use the checkpoint's supported settings and evaluate representative tasks; some extension methods require additional training. This calculation is not a complete model-specific extension algorithm or a performance benchmark.
context/storage discussion
21 / What must a KV cache preserve when using RoPE?
Explain reuse, original positions, and the double-rotation failure.

A key/value cache stores previously computed keys and values so generation can reuse the prefix rather than recomputing it. In a common implementation, each key is rotated using its original position before caching; its value is stored without that direct RoPE rotation. New queries continue with the correct next position. Other storage layouts are possible, but each comparison must apply the correct positional transform exactly once.
With the separate toy rate pi/4, raw key
. Rotating the already-rotated key by its position angle again turns it into
; the dot incorrectly becomes 1. Cache reuse preserves work, not an entitlement to unlimited context.
The cache lesson also traces the incorrect-index-reset case
16. Numbers become useful through objectives and contracts
Identify. Retrieve. Learn. Locate. Compare.
IDs are addresses; embedding values are trainable parameters.
A prediction objective supplies gradients; training updates shared rows, ordinary inference does not.
Dot products, norms, cosine, and distance measure declared geometry, not truth.
Offsets can be useful empirical hypotheses, never universal semantic equations.
Contextual hidden states differ from table rows; whole-text embeddings require a specified encoder/output procedure.
Sinusoidal and learned position vectors can be added to inputs; standard RoPE rotates query/key pairs instead.
Masking restricts visibility; correct cache positions preserve comparisons during generation.
Calculating another position is not evidence of useful unlimited context.
You can now trace the numerical boundary between a token address and a useful representation, and explain why position belongs to the model's computation rather than the ID. Continue to
From Inputs to Predictions: How Neural Networks Learn
to calculate a whole network's prediction and parameter update, then recognize its operations inside Transformer building blocks.

The vectors and scores are teaching examples, not measured production embeddings or API results. Pooling and positional calculations do not establish retrieval quality or usable context length. Complete embedding-model training, context-extension implementations, and a production semantic-search system require separate treatment and evaluation.

From Inputs to Predictions: How Neural Networks Learn
Calculate a network's prediction, follow the error backward, update every parameter, and recognize the same operations inside a Transformer.
Prerequisite: arithmetic; chapters 01-04 refreshed as needed
Original diagrams + complete training arithmetic

Your support service estimates resolution effort from ticket measurements. You can write rules, but the useful combinations keep changing. How can examples determine the coefficients of a prediction program? What actually changes when that program learns?

A neural network is a program built from numerical operations with adjustable values. In this chapter you will execute a small one by hand. Then you will use that experience to distinguish the jobs of attention, a feed-forward network, residual connections, and normalization inside a language model.

No mathematical background beyond arithmetic is assumed. The notation reminders link to fuller earlier lessons. Work through sections 1-7 in order: they form one prediction-to-update story. Sections 8-12 connect it to Transformers; sections 13-15 consolidate it, including
14 interview questions with explained answers

All features, weights, probabilities, and network widths below are invented teaching values, not measurements from a production service or model. They illustrate calculations, not a validated effort estimator or a benchmark.
1. Examples adjust a function, not the laws of arithmetic
A rule-based estimator might say, "Add extra effort whenever a ticket involves two services." You choose the rule and the number that controls how much effort to add. That number is a
. A learned estimator adjusts coefficients using example tickets and their observed outcomes. It needs a rule for measuring prediction mistakes; we will define one in section 5.
You still choose what to measure, how to build the model, how to train it, and how to evaluate it. Learning adjusts numbers within that design. It does not replace engineering judgment.

A neural network composes many such functions, including nonlinear ones. A
